title: HE CALLED HIMSELF A MAN OF GOD… UNTIL HIS EMPLOYEES BEGAN TALKING ABOUT HOW HE TREATED THEM.
paragraphs: HE CALLED HIMSELF A MAN OF GOD… UNTIL HIS EMPLOYEES BEGAN TALKING ABOUT HOW HE TREATED THEM.

He raised his hands in worship on Sunday. By Monday, the people working under him were praying just to survive another day. And the most frightening part of this story isn't what his employees said about him. It's what Jesus might say.
Nobody questioned his Christianity.
Not at first.

He posted Bible verses almost every morning. His social media profile proudly declared, “Jesus is Lord.” He donated to church projects, spoke passionately about faith, and never missed an opportunity to tell people how God had blessed his business.
When someone complimented his success, he smiled.
“All glory to God.”
And people believed him.
Why wouldn't they?
He knew Scripture. He spoke confidently about prayer. He could explain the importance of obedience, generosity, and Christian leadership.
But there was something the congregation never saw.
Something his employees knew all too well.
Because behind the office doors, the same man who spoke about God's love could make another human being feel utterly worthless.
And eventually, the people who worked for him began talking.
Not because they wanted to destroy his reputation.
But because they were exhausted from trying to survive it.
And here is the question that should make every Christian uncomfortable:
What if the people who know us outside the church are telling a completely different story about the Jesus we claim to represent?
Before you decide this story is about someone else, keep reading.
Because sometimes the most dangerous spiritual blindness is not failing to recognize sin in another person.
It is becoming so familiar with our own religious appearance that we stop examining the condition of our hearts.
The following workplace story is an illustrative composite, not an accusation against an identifiable individual. But the spiritual problem it exposes is painfully real.
One employee had been working there for years.
She was dependable. Rarely complained. Often stayed late when deadlines became impossible.

At home, she had responsibilities no one in the office fully understood. Bills waiting. Family members depending on her. Nights when she calculated how much money would remain after groceries and electricity.
She needed that job.
And her employer knew it.
One morning, she made a mistake.
Not a dishonest mistake. Not an act of rebellion.
A human mistake.
The kind almost everyone makes when overwhelmed.
But instead of correcting her privately and helping her understand what went wrong, her employer humiliated her in front of her coworkers.
His voice grew louder.
His words became sharper.
She tried to explain.
He interrupted.
She apologized.
He continued.
By the time it ended, she was fighting tears.
And the man who had publicly thanked God for his company's success returned to his office as though nothing unusual had happened.
That evening, she sat in her car before driving home.
Her hands were still trembling.
She looked at her reflection in the rearview mirror and whispered something heartbreaking.
“Lord, am I really that useless?”
Think about that.
A woman who had spent the day trying to earn a living was now asking God whether she had any worth.
Not because God had rejected her.
But because someone claiming to represent Him had treated her as though she were disposable.
And somewhere else, her employer was preparing another inspirational Christian post.
Perhaps you know what that feels like.
Perhaps you've worked for someone who spoke beautifully about God but treated people cruelly when no one important was watching.
Perhaps you were the employee who cried in the restroom, wiped your face, and returned to work because your family needed the paycheck.
Or perhaps you are reading this with an uncomfortable realization.
You have never been that employee.
You have been the employer.
The supervisor.
The manager.
The parent.
The ministry leader.
The person whose words carried enough authority to make someone afraid.
And you have called your behavior “discipline,” “high standards,” or “leadership,” when deep down you knew some of it was anger, pride, impatience, or the need to control.
If that possibility makes you uncomfortable, don't run from it.
Sometimes conviction is the beginning of mercy.
Because Scripture has something to say about the distance between a person's religious reputation and the way they treat people.
And it is far more serious than most of us realize.
In Colossians 4:1, the apostle Paul writes:
The original Greek contains the expression:
τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὴν ἰσότητα
to dikaion kai tēn isotēta
Meaning, in context, what is just and fair.
Paul was addressing masters and enslaved people within the social world of the Roman Empire. We should not pretend that ancient slavery was identical to modern employment. It was not.
But the moral force of Paul's command remains unmistakable.
People who possess authority are accountable to the Lord for how they exercise it.
Power does not cancel justice.
Position does not excuse cruelty.
And claiming to serve God does not give anyone permission to mistreat those under their authority.
Notice something else.
Paul does not merely tell those with power to be religious.
He commands them to practice justice and fairness.
Then he reminds them that they, too, have a Master.
A heavenly Master.
Someone whose authority is infinitely greater than theirs.
Imagine how differently a workplace would operate if every Christian employer remembered that the people beneath their organizational authority are never beneath their human dignity.
Imagine a supervisor pausing before shouting because he remembers that Christ hears his words.
Imagine a business owner examining wages, workloads, and working conditions because he understands that profitability does not erase accountability.
Imagine a manager realizing that the employee standing nervously in front of his desk is someone made in the image of God.
Because that is exactly what Scripture teaches.
Genesis 1:27 declares that God created humanity in His image.
In Hebrew, the expression is:
בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים
b'tselem Elohim
“In the image of God.”
That truth does not disappear when someone puts on a uniform.
It does not disappear when someone earns minimum wage.
It does not disappear when someone makes a mistake.
It does not disappear because an employer pays their salary.
A person's dignity is not a benefit granted by a company.
It is rooted in the God who created them.
And when we forget that, something spiritually dangerous begins happening.
We start treating people as instruments of our ambitions instead of neighbors we are commanded to love.
We begin measuring their worth by productivity.
We demand patience when we make mistakes but offer little mercy when they do.
We expect loyalty without practicing fairness.
We call ourselves blessed while the people helping us build our success quietly suffer.
And then we wonder why the world sometimes struggles to believe our testimony.
But Jesus already warned us about this kind of contradiction.
In Matthew 23:27, He rebuked religious leaders who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
He compared them to whitewashed tombs.
Beautiful on the outside.
But inwardly filled with death and uncleanness.
Those words were spoken in a particular confrontation with religious hypocrisy. They were not a blanket condemnation of every religious leader.
Still, the warning reaches into every generation.
Because religious appearances can become dangerously convincing.
A person can learn the vocabulary of holiness without surrendering the habits of pride.
A person can give money publicly while withholding compassion privately.
A person can defend biblical truth in an argument while refusing to practice biblical love in a relationship.
A person can know exactly when to say “Praise the Lord” and still refuse to say “I was wrong.”
And that last sentence may expose more than we want to admit.
Because repentance is not proven by how passionately we condemn the sins of other people.
It is revealed in what we do when God confronts our own.
James 3:9–10 describes the contradiction of using the tongue to bless God while cursing human beings made in God's likeness.
James concludes:
“My brethren, these things ought not so to be.” (KJV)
Not “these things are understandable because leadership is stressful.”
Not “these things are acceptable because the business is profitable.”
Not “these things are excusable because the person is generous at church.”
They ought not so to be.
That is the uncomfortable clarity of Scripture.
And perhaps the most devastating detail in our story is this:
The employees were not asking their employer to become perfect.
They were asking him to become humane.
They wanted correction without humiliation.
Accountability without intimidation.
Expectations without constant fear.
A workplace where honesty was not punished and exhaustion was not mistaken for laziness.
Some wanted fair compensation.
Others wanted reasonable workloads.
Some simply wanted to be spoken to with dignity.
And several had stopped believing that bringing their concerns forward would change anything.
Then one day, an employee finally spoke.
Not loudly.
Not disrespectfully.
Just honestly.
“Sir, you always tell us you're a man of God. But sometimes we're afraid to come to work because of how you treat us.”
The room became quiet.
And for the first time, the employer had to face a question his success had helped him avoid.
What if the people who worked closest to him were seeing something his church friends never saw?
What if his employees knew his temper better than his congregation knew his testimony?
What if the people he paid were suffering under behavior that contradicted the Lord he praised?
He could have defended himself.
He could have reminded them that he owned the business.
He could have listed everything he had done for them.
He could have accused them of being ungrateful.
He could have reached for a Bible verse about obedience while ignoring the verses about his own responsibilities.
And that is where this story becomes about more than one employer.
Because every one of us eventually encounters a moment when the truth threatens the version of ourselves we prefer to believe.
The question is not whether we have ever failed.
Romans 3:23 tells us that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
The question is what we do when our failure is exposed.
Do we become defensive?
Do we punish the messenger?
Do we hide behind religious language?
Or do we allow the truth to lead us toward repentance?
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia).
It speaks of a change of mind or heart, a reorientation that, in biblical repentance, bears fruit in changed conduct.
It is not simply embarrassment because someone discovered what we did.
It is not regret because our reputation suffered.
And it is certainly not an emotional apology designed to end an uncomfortable conversation.
Biblical repentance turns away from sin and toward God.
It takes responsibility.
It seeks to repair what can be repaired.
And it stops demanding that wounded people pretend the wounds never happened.
That distinction matters.
Because an employer can apologize on Friday and resume humiliating employees on Monday.
A pastor can preach about humility and still refuse correction.
A husband can ask forgiveness without abandoning controlling behavior.
A Christian can cry during worship without allowing the Holy Spirit to change how they treat their family.
Tears can accompany repentance.
But tears alone do not prove it.
John the Baptist said in Luke 3:8:
“Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance.” (KJV)
And when people asked him what that meant, his answers became remarkably practical.
Share with those in need.
Do not collect more than you are authorized to collect.
Do not extort.
Be content with your wages.
In other words, repentance was never intended to remain an invisible religious feeling.
It was meant to change how people lived.
How they handled money.
How they exercised authority.
How they treated their neighbors.
How they behaved when personal advantage tempted them to do wrong.
And if that was true in the days of John the Baptist, why would it be less true in a modern workplace?
Consider another passage.
James 5:4 says:

“Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.” (KJV)
The Greek expression is:
κυρίου σαβαώθ
kyriou sabaōth
“Lord of hosts.”
The title invokes God's sovereign power, drawing on the Hebrew יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH tseva'ot), often rendered “LORD of hosts.”
James was specifically condemning wealthy oppressors who fraudulently withheld wages from laborers.
That context matters.
We should not use the passage to claim that every disagreement over compensation is automatically wage theft.
But where wages are deliberately withheld through fraud, Scripture does not treat the matter as a minor business inconvenience.
It declares that the cries of exploited workers reach the Lord of hosts.
Think about that.
The employee whose wages were withheld may have no influence.
The worker who fears retaliation may have no powerful connections.
The laborer who cannot afford legal representation may feel completely invisible.
But Scripture refuses to call that person invisible to God.
The Lord hears.
And the same God who hears prayers offered in beautiful sanctuaries also hears the cries of people suffering injustice.
That should comfort the oppressed.
And sober anyone entrusted with authority.
But now we must go deeper.
Because the Gospel is not merely a warning against becoming a cruel employer.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and transform human hearts.
Including hearts corrupted by pride.
Including hearts hardened by success.
Including hearts that have used religion as a shield against accountability.
Including yours.
Including mine.
And this is where the story changes.
Because if all we do is expose hypocrisy, we may leave people feeling condemned without showing them the Savior.
And Jesus did not come merely to expose the darkness.
He came as the Light of the world.
In Luke 19, we meet Zacchaeus.
A wealthy chief tax collector.
A man associated with a system in which tax collectors could exploit others for personal gain.
He was not presented as someone whose social standing automatically proved righteousness.
Yet Jesus stopped beneath the tree where Zacchaeus had climbed and called him by name.
Jesus entered his home.
And grace began confronting the life he had been living.
Then something remarkable happened.
Zacchaeus declared:
“Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold.” (Luke 19:8, KJV)
Do not miss the beauty of that moment.
He did not simply announce that he had become more religious.
He did not ask the crowd to forget his past because he had met Jesus.
He did not use grace as permission to keep whatever he had unjustly gained.
His response included generosity and restitution.
He was willing to confront the financial consequences of wrongdoing.
And Jesus declared that salvation had come to his house.
Then came one of the most beautiful statements in all of Scripture:
“For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.” (Luke 19:10, KJV)
There it is.
The heart of the Gospel.
Jesus seeks the lost.
Not merely the respectable.
Not merely the publicly admired.
Not merely the people whose reputations remain spotless.
He seeks sinners.
And when His saving grace takes hold of a life, it does not teach us to celebrate the sins from which He came to redeem us.
It teaches us to turn from them.
Zacchaeus did not purchase salvation through restitution.
His response demonstrated the transforming power of grace.
That distinction is essential.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by our works, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
Yet the very next verse tells us that we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
Grace is not a transaction in which we earn God's acceptance by becoming morally impressive.
Grace is God's undeserved favor in Christ, bringing forgiveness and new life that produces the fruit of obedience.
So what would repentance look like for the employer in our story?
Perhaps it would begin with a sentence he had never learned to say sincerely.
“I have sinned against God in how I treated you.”
No excuses.
No “I'm sorry if you were offended.”
No blaming stress, business pressure, or difficult personalities.
Just responsibility.
Perhaps he would invite employees to speak without fear of punishment.
Perhaps he would discover that some had endured far more than he realized.
Perhaps he would have to repay withheld wages, correct unfair practices, establish meaningful protections against retaliation, or seek independent accountability.
Perhaps some employees would decide to leave anyway.
And he would have to accept that.
Because repentance does not entitle us to immediate forgiveness from those we have wounded.
Nor does forgiveness automatically restore trust.
Trust may require time, consistent conduct, and accountability.
And some relationships cannot safely return to what they were.
That does not mean grace has failed.
It means grace is not the same as pretending harm never happened.
Sometimes the most honest evidence of repentance is accepting consequences without resentment.
Sometimes it is listening without defending yourself.
Sometimes it is making restitution even when nobody is watching.
Sometimes it is stepping away from authority until you have demonstrated that you can exercise it responsibly.
And sometimes it is finally understanding that the people you hurt were never obstacles to your success.
They were human beings you were commanded to love.

Jesus said in Mark 10:43–45 that greatness among His followers must be expressed through service, pointing to His own mission as the Son of Man who came not to be served but to serve and give His life as a ransom for many.
The cross overturns our worldly understanding of power.
The King of kings did not come demanding that suffering humanity make Him comfortable.
He humbled Himself.
He served.
He gave Himself.
He bore sin.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way for sinners to be reconciled to God.
That is the Lord Christian leaders claim to follow.
Not a Savior who used authority to crush the vulnerable.
But the Savior who laid down His life.
Now imagine the employer standing at the foot of that cross.
Not holding his business awards.
Not displaying his donation receipts.
Not rehearsing his religious accomplishments.
Just standing there.
A sinner in need of mercy.
The same mercy his employees needed him to show.
And imagine finally understanding that the greatest testimony he could offer was not another carefully written Christian caption.
It was a changed life.
A gentler answer.
A fairer workplace.
An honest apology.
A corrected injustice.
A willingness to serve.
A heart no longer desperate to be admired.
Because Jesus does not merely improve our public image.
He makes us new.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.” (KJV)
This does not promise instant moral perfection.
Christians continue to battle sin and need ongoing repentance.
But it does proclaim the reality of new life in Christ.
And new life must eventually touch the places where our old ways have caused pain.
For the employer, that includes the office.
For the pastor, the congregation.
For the parent, the home.
For the spouse, the marriage.
For the Christian business owner, the people who help keep the business alive.
And for every believer, the people who encounter us when there is no audience to impress.
Maybe you are reading this as someone who has been hurt by a person claiming to be godly.
Please hear this carefully.
Their cruelty does not define Jesus.
Their hypocrisy does not invalidate the Gospel.
And their misuse of Scripture does not mean God approves of what happened to you.
You are not required to remain in an abusive workplace to prove your faith.
You are not disobeying Christ by documenting mistreatment, seeking appropriate help, reporting unlawful conduct, or establishing necessary boundaries.
Forgiveness is not permission for someone to keep harming you.
And Christian humility does not require surrendering your God-given dignity.
The Jesus who calls sinners to repentance is also the Jesus who cares for the wounded.
He sees what others overlook.
He knows the prayers you whispered after difficult days.
He knows how hard it was to keep showing up when you felt small.
And though healing may take time, His grace is not beyond your reach.
But perhaps you are on the other side of this story.
Perhaps you have been the one whose words wounded people.
Perhaps you recognize the impatience, the pride, the need to dominate, the tendency to excuse harshness because you carry responsibility.
Then hear the invitation of Christ.
You do not have to keep hiding behind the image of a good Christian.
You can confess your sin.
You can turn away from it.
You can seek forgiveness from God through Jesus Christ.
You can take responsibility for the people you have harmed.
You can begin making things right.
First John 1:9 tells believers that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because Jesus Christ is sufficient.
His sacrifice is greater than the shame you have been hiding.
His mercy is greater than your carefully protected reputation.
And His transforming grace is powerful enough to confront the habits you thought would never change.
But do not confuse being forgiven with being excused from obedience.
If you have wronged someone, do what is right.
If you have withheld what belongs to them, restore it.
If you have used your position to intimidate, stop.
If you have cultivated a workplace of fear, begin the difficult work of changing it.
If you have spoken about Christ while refusing to resemble His humility, repent.
Not to earn salvation.
But because the Savior who forgives also calls us to follow Him.
And if you're wondering whether this message is meant for you, consider one final question.
If the people who experience you at your worst were asked what kind of Christian you are, would their answer resemble the testimony you give about yourself?
That question is not meant to destroy you.
It is meant to invite honest examination before God.
Because sometimes the most important testimony is not the one we give with a microphone.
It is the one other people experience through our conduct.
The employee who is corrected with patience.
The cleaner greeted with respect.
The struggling worker treated with compassion.
The person who receives the wages they are owed.
The exhausted mother who is allowed to speak without being humiliated.
The colleague whose dignity is protected even when they make a mistake.
These things may never go viral.
They may never earn applause.
They may never appear in a church testimony video.
But they matter to God.
And when we fail, the answer is not to abandon the name of Jesus.
It is to return to Jesus in repentance and faith.
Because Christianity is not a performance for people who have mastered the appearance of holiness.
It is a life of following the crucified and risen Savior who calls sinners out of darkness into His marvelous light.
This is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to build a community of people who merely know how to sound Christian.
But to keep pointing hearts toward Scripture, repentance, forgiveness, discipleship, and genuine transformation through Jesus Christ.
If this story reminded you of something you have endured, or something you need to change, you do not have to pretend it did not touch you.
You do not need to explain your private pain publicly.
But you are welcome to share your testimony or a lesson God has been teaching you. Your words may encourage someone who has been suffering in silence.
Not to embarrass or accuse a particular person.
But because someone in your circle may need the courage to seek help, the humility to repent, or the reminder that Jesus has not abandoned them.
These resources are intended to help believers become more rooted in Scripture, more discerning in faith, and more faithful in everyday life.
And if this ministry has been spiritually helpful to you, I want to extend a personal invitation.
Not because paying a ministry earns forgiveness, salvation, favor, or spiritual blessing.
And not because you are obligated to give money to prove you love Jesus.
You are not.
Salvation is God's gift through Christ.
But Scripture does encourage voluntary, cheerful generosity in support of faithful ministry.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be done reluctantly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
But the deeper invitation is not about merchandise.
It is about participating in the work of putting Christ-centered truth before people who desperately need it.
Some are struggling to pray.
Some have been wounded by religious hypocrisy.
Some are drifting from their faith.
Some have never understood the Gospel clearly.
Some are outwardly successful but inwardly exhausted.
And some are one honest encounter with Scripture away from beginning a life-changing journey of repentance and faith.
We cannot manufacture conversion.
Only God can change the heart.
But we can faithfully proclaim His Word, make biblical resources accessible, and encourage one another to keep following Jesus.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share biblical truth matters.
Your faithfulness to Jesus matters.
The Gospel is not for sale.
So before you close this article, return to that employee sitting alone in her car.
Remember her trembling hands.
Remember the question she whispered.
“Lord, am I really that useless?”
Now imagine what could have happened if her employer had understood the Gospel not merely as something to proclaim, but as truth that should transform the way he exercised authority.
Perhaps he would have corrected her mistake without crushing her spirit.
Perhaps he would have recognized the burdens she was carrying.
Perhaps he would have remembered that the woman sitting across from him was made in God's image.
Perhaps he would have spoken to her the way he hoped his own family would be treated.
And perhaps she would have driven home that evening without wondering whether she mattered.
That is not a small thing.
Because the way we treat people can leave wounds that outlast our words.
And the way we follow Christ can become a living witness to the grace we proclaim.
The employer in this story began with a reputation for being a man of God.
But the question that mattered was whether he would allow God to change the man behind the reputation.
That question belongs to all of us.
We can protect the image.
Or we can surrender the heart.
We can keep defending the old life.
Or we can follow the Savior who makes all things new.
And when we fail, we can come back to the cross, where the holiness of God confronts our sin and the mercy of God meets repentant sinners through Jesus Christ.
Because no amount of religious applause can replace genuine obedience.
And no scandal is beyond the redeeming power of Christ when a sinner truly turns to Him.
The people you wounded may never remember your favorite Bible verse, but they will remember whether your life gave them a reason to believe you took Jesus seriously.
